#### Foreword

Katherine Allen first studied Tai Chi and Qigong with me in 1988. Since that time she has made a deep study of internal therapeutic arts including Daoyin (leading and conducting), Tuina (Chinese massage) and yoga. She has trained with leading teachers from all over the world. As a Qigong therapist, Katherine is highly experienced in treating clients with a wide variety of problems and has conducted classes for the elderly and for psychiatric patients. She is a warm and empathetic person with a wonderful sense of humour. I can think of no better guide to introduce the reader to the mysteries of Qigong.
Dan Docherty

#### Introduction

Most of us want to live a healthy life, with a peaceful mind and spirit. There are many ways to achieve this and Qigong is one excellent way.
This book is intended to be a broad outline of the more valuable aspects of Qigong and I hope that it will encourage you to take up this beneficial mind and body practice. Some topics that may deserve volumes of explanation have been summarized to provide you with an overview of a boundlessly interesting subject. However, at the end of the book, there are suggestions for further reading if you wish to deepen your understanding and practice of Qigong.
There is no need to start at the beginning of the book. If you wish to try any Qigong exercise right away, simply turn to the appropriate page for that exercise and check it out, as each section has been carefully laid out to make this possible. Although it would increase your understanding to look at the chapter What Makes Qigong Different from Other Exercise? and the Posture and Movement Principles chapter before starting, that’s up to you. Some people like to dive in and learn as they go, while others prefer to have some preparatory knowledge first. This book has been written with both learning styles in mind and is constructed to enable you to “cherry pick” selected exercises, depending on what you feel is needed on any particular day.
Early morning Qigong practice. Group performing Drawing the Bow.
In my years of teaching Qigong, I have been delighted to observe many hundreds of people become fitter, more supple, better balanced, calmer and more able to cope with everyday problems, as a result of their Qigong practice. Qigong encourages a feeling of flow, which calms the nervous system and stimulates all the life processes of the body. It can be adapted for every ability and health condition. Even a small amount of regular practice brings health benefits as well as enjoyment and a sense of wellbeing.
There are thousands of different Qigong exercises and many variations of each exercise. In this book I have presented a carefully selected series of Qigong exercises, chosen for their comprehensively wide-ranging appeal and usefulness to the new or relatively new student. As any Qigong master will tell you, trying to learn every movement as quickly as possible is counterproductive. If you just relax, take advantage of the way the book is arranged, and start with some of the moves that appeal to you, the benefits will accrue naturally.
The good news is that all Qigong exercises follow the same basic principles, and putting these principles into action is what produces the beneficial results. Quantity is not important. Practising just your personally chosen selection of the exercises might well be enough to improve your general wellbeing.

##### The relationship between Qigong and Taiji

Qigong and Taiji (also known as Tai Chi) operate from the same general principles and offer similar benefits. The beginnings of Qigong date back five thousand years. Taiji was developed much later, in the 14th century, so you could look upon Qigong as the wellspring and Taiji as the offspring.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Pushing a Door Qigong.
A Taiji form is a series of carefully devised moves derived from its original purpose, which was self-defence. The moves are linked in a long, flowing sequence, which has many of the same qualities as dance and which takes the average person considerable time to learn. Some teachers view the Taiji form to be a long, intricate Qigong sequence.
A Qigong move can be so simple that you can learn it in five minutes. There are some Qigong styles that involve numerous complicated moves linked together, but these more complex sets are not suitable for this book. Many Qigong exercises are used for self-defence, but others are simply for health.

##### What do you need to start Qigong?

Loose or stretchy clothing – wear anything that is comfortable and allows unrestricted movement. You don’t need a fancy silk suit (unless of course you want one!).
Flat, flexible shoes – with thin soles that allow you to feel the ground under your feet and are roomy enough to wriggle your toes. Bare feet are also fine where the floor surface is safe. The Chinese usually practise outdoors and wearing shoes is traditional.
A small area of space – indoors or out, at any time of day. The Chinese like to practise outside early in the morning when the energy of the earth is strongest, under trees if possible, and again at dusk.
A smile on your face – no need to get too serious, as this just tenses up your body and mind.
Hey presto, you are ready to start!
SPELLING OF CHINESE WORDS
The Pinyin spelling system has been used to transcribe the sounds of Mandarin Chinese throughout this book. In the late 1970s, China asked the United Nations to adopt the Pinyin system as the international standard for phonetic transcription of Chinese. It is now used worldwide, following approval by the United Nations and the International Organization for Standardization.
In the past, words like Qigong were spelled as ch’i kung (Wade Giles system), chi gung (Yale system) or some other variation.
With Pinyin, there is a choice of separating syllables or joining them. For example, both Qi gong and Qigong are used. However, joining syllables is usually more helpful, both for word sense and for looking up words in a Chinese dictionary.

#### What Is Qigong?

Qigong is a Chinese system of holistic health practice, with roots dating back five thousand years. “Energy cultivation” is an excellent translation for Qigong, because it conveys the idea that, just as an agricultural field is cultivated with careful tending over time to produce food, your own field of life energy is cultivated so that your body and mind are nourished.
Qigong brings body, breathing and mind together to perform movements and hold postures that exercise the whole person. While usually performed standing, it can also be performed seated. Although most Qigong is characterized by slow, flowing movements, it can also be still.
The art of Qigong is an effective method of reducing stress and promoting a relaxed body and calm mind. It increases flexibility, strength, balance and general wellbeing. Many people have found that Qigong practice brings youthful vitality and a positive outlook to their lives.
There is a Chinese saying that the “Yi leads the Qi”. Yi is a calm, focused mind, full of intention. First, allow your body and mind to relax so that tension, unnecessary muscle action and superfluous mental activity do not get in the way. Next, bring your mind into a perfect state of attention in the present moment, which will allow you to develop the ability to move effortlessly and feel the flow of life energy through your body.
Qigong is suitable for any age, any ability and any type of personality. It can be adapted to fit any need. No one is excluded.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Chinese characters for Qigong, pronounced “cheegong”.
QI + GONG
The word Qigong is made up of two Chinese words:
Qi = air, energy, spirit, vigour, atmosphere, attitude
Gong = achievement, merit, result, effect, success, skill
At one with nature.

#### The History of Qigong

The beginnings of Qigong emerged some five thousand years ago. Archaeologists have found ancient Chinese rock art in caves, depicting men in standing postures, similar to the standing Qigong we use today.
Chinese philosophers, alchemists and emperors have a long history of searching for the elixir of life. Some sought a potion or pill for immortality. Other seekers devoted their lives to finding an internal elixir, using special teachings and complex practices to transform a person’s internal alchemy.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Daoyin Tu silk scroll, c. 168 BCE, discovered in a tomb in China in 1973.
Qigong is a relatively modern word and was not in use until the 20th century. Many terms were used before that, for example Xingqi (promoting the circulation of Qi), Fuqi (taking Qi), Daoyin (guiding the energy flow), Tuna (exhaling and inhaling), Yangshen (nourishing the spirit) and Jingzuo (sitting still). In the 1970s the Chinese government began to use the term Qigong officially and it now refers to all self-healing exercise and meditation techniques from ancient times to the present.
From early times, there have been many written references to Qigong. In Chapter 10 of the Daoist classic Daodejing (The Way and Its Power) by Laozi (c. 6th century BCE), we find:
By harmonizing the Yang and Yin
and embracing The One,
you become unified.
By concentrating the Qi (vitality)
and inducing tenderness and purity,
you become supple and free like a little child.
This ideal of achieving the suppleness of a child, the bending ability of bamboo or a young sapling, in order to become resilient and in harmony with the flow of life, runs through all Daoist thinking.
In 1973 archaeologists excavating the tomb of King Ma (c. 168 BCE) near the city of Changsha, the capital of Hunan province, found a folded piece of silk in one of the coffins. This silk scroll, the Daoyin Tu, depicted the earliest drawings found to date of Daoyin postures, a traditional form of Chinese exercise. The scroll contained 44 figures painted on silk: men and women of different ages, wearing clothes from different walks of life, from peasant to government official. This suggests that therapeutic exercise was practised by all types of people.
It could be argued that Qigong, with both its documented research and its tradition of health and longevity, is the closest anyone has come to finding the “golden elixir of life”.

#### Internal Alchemy

To the ancient Daoist sages, the human body had a symbolic inner landscape that related to the outer landscape of the world around them. The Chart of Internal Alchemy depicts a side view of a man seated in meditation, with an inner landscape of stars, mountains, rivers, forests, pathways and people. It represents important knowledge of how the inner landscape works to purify the body and spirit in order to cultivate health, longevity and one’s inner nature, with the ultimate goals being immortality and spiritual transcendence. The earliest records of such symbology are estimated to date from around the 10th century.

##### Symbolism in the Chart of Internal Alchemy

Symbolism in the Lower Dantian: At the lower part of the spine, a girl and boy (Yin and Yang) are working on a treadmill. They are trying to invert the course of Jing and thereby preserve it. On their right, a fiery furnace creates heat to transform the watery Jing into steam and send it upward. A little further up, a hard-working ox is ploughing the earth in preparation for the planting of the first seed for the cultivation of the golden elixir.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
The Neijing Tu, The Chart of Internal Alchemy. This illustration is based on a stone engraving from 1886 found at the White Clouds Monastery, Beijing.
Symbolism in the Middle Dantian: On the top of the round spiral shape, which represents the Middle Dantian, stands the Herd Boy. He holds the seven-star constellation of Ursa Major, which the Chinese refer to as The Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper. This is a constellation rich in Daoist mythologies and is a symbol of the centre of the cosmos. The Weaving Maiden sits below at her loom, near the kidneys. There is a famous Chinese story in which the Herd Boy (Yang) meets the Weaving Maiden (Yin) once each year to join the energies of Yin and Yang.
Symbolism in the Upper Dantian: Nine mountain peaks are at the top of the head, representing Yang energy and the highest point we can climb toward heaven while bound to earth. The monk who brought Chan Buddhism to China in the 6th century, Bodhidharma (Da Mo), is shown standing, with both arms stretched toward heaven. Above him in black robes, seated in meditation, is the ancient sage Laozi, who is said to hold the secret of eternal truth. The two dots between Bodhidharma and Laozi represent the sun and moon and also the eyes of the meditator.
There are many complex symbologies contained within the Chart of Internal Alchemy alluding to secret methods of transforming Jing into Qi into Shen and ultimately into divine energy, with the final goal being immortality.
To understand more of the meaning of the picture, we must look briefly at the Three Dantians and the Three Treasures.

##### The Three Dantians

The word Dantian is translated as Cinnabar Field. This implies the elixir of life, because cinnabar is mercuric sulphide and was an important ingredient in elixir of life potions and pills used in External Alchemy.
There are three major Dantians: Lower, Middle and Upper. However, if someone talks about “The Dantian”, they are usually referring to the Lower Dantian.
The Lower Dantian: This is located approximately two fingers’ width below and behind the navel at your physical centre of gravity. This Dantian is used as a focal point in Qigong practice and in martial arts. The Lower Dantian is your main energy reservoir and place of physical strength, stamina and stability. It is also the core of your “gut feelings”, which cannot be explained by logic but which we learn to trust as we become more connected to this energy centre. As this Dantian is closest to the earth, it is the most Yin of the three Dantians. In Qigong we complete our practice by symbolically gathering up the Qi energy with our hands and arms, moving them in a circular motion of collecting and bringing our hands, full of Qi, to rest at the Dantian.
The Three Dantians.
The Middle Dantian: This is located behind the breast bone, at heart level. The Middle Dantian is your centre of emotion, empathy, compassion and love. Empathy allows you to communicate emotionally with others. If the heart area is relaxed and open, it is easier to relate to all living things. Balancing the Middle Dantian allows us to heal any emotional disorders that we might be carrying. When we practise Qigong, there are many exercises that open the chest area to allow the practitioner to feel emotionally free and at ease.
The Upper Dantian: This is located between the eyebrows, behind your forehead. The Upper Dantian is associated with intuition, higher intellect and spirituality, and it is often favoured in Qigong meditation because of its spiritual significance. This Dantian is looked upon as a gateway to divine transformation.
No individual Dantian has the capability of functioning on its own, in isolation from the others. For example, if you do not have the foundational strength and stability that the Lower Dantian provides, you will have no ability to energize and steady your heart and your head. If you do not have the compassion of the heart from the Middle Dantian, your Lower Dantian strength will become overbearing and lack the gentleness needed to deal with others and yourself. If you do not have the higher intellect of the Upper Dantian, your strength, courage and emotion will not be intelligently directed. The Three Dantians must work in harmony for us to be balanced.
In Qigong practice, we employ flowing movement, correct breathing, correct posture, efficient use of energy, relaxation, concentration, calmness, intention of purpose and understanding of our body, mind and emotions to achieve a balance of the Three Dantians for the purpose of engendering health, vitality and mental clarity.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
If Jing is compared to the wax and wick of the candle and Qi to the candle flame, then Shen is the light and radiance given off by the flame.

##### The Three Treasures

The Three Treasures are Jing, Qi and Shen. Jing is life essence and vitality; Qi is breath and energy; Shen is mind and spirit. Jing, Qi and Shen are considered to be the Three Treasures of mankind, because their energies are essential to human life.
Jing: This belongs to the Lower Dantian. It is considered to be a Yin form of Qi, connected to earthly things and always moving downward, like water. Jing belongs to the material world. It is the germ of life, the reproductive energy of sperm and egg, the sexual secretions, the vigour of growth and vitality. Jing is influenced by our genes, nutrition and lifestyle choices.
Qi: This belongs to the Middle Dantian. When viewed in relationship to Jing and Shen, Qi is considered neutral, neither Yin nor Yang in itself, but capable of functioning in either capacity. Qi moves in all directions. Qi is air, breath and life-force energy, and it affects all of our life processes.
Shen: This belongs to the Upper Dantian. Shen is considered to be a Yang form of Qi, connected to heavenly things and always moving upward, like fire. Shen is mind and spirit, and it affects our senses and nervous system. Our Shen is said to shine in the light of our eyes. When we reach a state of clarity in meditation, we nourish Shen.
Qigong exercises and meditation conserve, circulate and balance Jing, Qi and Shen.

##### Internal Alchemy in modern practice

The lasting impression of the Chart of Internal Alchemy for me is the fact that for over a thousand years, possibly much longer, Chinese culture has embraced ways of nurturing health, vitality, longevity and wisdom. They have journeyed inside themselves to use existing physical, mental and spiritual energies. Qigong can be part of this inner transformation for the better, which makes Internal Alchemy relevant to everyone today.

#### Yin and Yang

To the ancient Chinese mind, we exist because earth has the perfect balance of Yin and Yang energies. Yin energy comes upward from the earth and is moist, cool and nurturing. Yang energy comes downward from the sky and is dry, warm and energizing. The “Qi” in Qigong means life energy. This life energy is a constantly alternating dance of Yin and Yang. When Yin and Yang interact, the physical world is created. When Yin and Yang are balanced in our bodies, health results and our Qi energy increases. Qigong exercises balance the energies of Yin and Yang within us through our meridian channels, throughout our body tissues and through our energy centres. Yin and Yang energies are always changing with the passage of time.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Embroidery interpretation of the Yin Yang symbol.
An understanding of Yin and Yang will add to your Qigong practice. In a healthy body, Yin Qi nurtures and Yang Qi energizes. When you breathe, your inhalation is Yin because you are bringing in Yin energy and nurturing the blood with oxygen. Your exhalation is Yang because you are exhaling heat and toxins and other waste products.
Whenever you move in Qigong, inward movements are Yin and outward movements are Yang. Downward movements are Yin and upward movements are Yang. Qigong movements travel through a complete cycle of Yin and Yang, and to reflect this cycle the movements are continuous, fluid and rounded.
Your body is viewed as having Yin and Yang aspects. The front of your body is Yin and the back is Yang. Your lower body is Yin and your upper body is Yang. The inside of your body is Yin and the outer surface is Yang. Your Yin organs are the liver, kidneys, lungs, spleen and heart, while your Yang organs are the gall bladder, small intestine, stomach, large intestine and triple burner. The Yin meridian channels are deeper, and the Yang meridians are nearer the surface.
Qigong cultivates a health-restoring balance of Yin and Yang energies.

##### The Yin Yang symbol

This well-known representation is also known as the Taijitu (supreme ultimate diagram). This image has an intrinsic elegance because it symbolizes a simple idea that can be endlessly complex. Though two-dimensional, the diagram could be thought of as three-dimensional. If you add the fourth dimension, to include time, then you could think of it as a process of transformation, moving through time.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Every civilization attempts to provide a coherent view of the world. The Chinese have done this through the philosophical concept that all creation started from nothing, became unity and then divided into Yin and Yang, ultimately giving birth to all things.
The first recorded mention of Yin and Yang was in the Classic of Changes, the Yijing, thought to have originated in 2000–3000 BCE. Right up to the present day, the concept has been an intrinsic part of Chinese philosophy, affecting the way in which art, music, medicine, health, diet, cooking and indeed all things in life are viewed.
Yin Yang philosophy is not the same as Western dualism. A diagram of the latter would be a circle with a line down the middle with one side black and the other white. There would be no dots of white and black in each side to represent an interchange or mutual dependency. Also, there would be interminable argument over which side were best. There is no such argument about the Yin Yang theory because one side cannot exist without the other.

##### Everything is relative

Cold is Yin and hot is Yang. However, what is being compared is always relative. If you were comparing hot to warm, then warm would be the more Yin of the two. A challenging Qigong move would be seen as Yang, and an easier, restorative move as Yin. However, this would all be a matter of degree. You might have two moves that are challenging, so both a Yang idea, but if one were less challenging, it would be Yin in relationship to the more challenging move.
This table shows a few Yin and Yang opposites.


##### Everything contains the seed of its opposite

In the middle of each half of the Yin Yang symbol is a dot. This symbolizes that within Yin is a measure of Yang, within Yang is a measure of Yin, and nothing is static. Yin and Yang are always influencing and changing each other. Night carries the seed of day. Day carries the seed of night. Spring carries the seed of Summer, which carries the seed of Autumn, which carries the seed of Winter, until the cycle begins again. The dot symbolizes the potential and ability to change and rebalance to create equilibrium. When we exhale, the ability to inhale is there waiting. When we expend energy, the ability to recharge our energy is there waiting. When we stretch out an arm or leg, we never extend any joint to its maximum; that little dot of Yin softness in every joint is what allows our movement to be fluid and ever-changing without any stiffness.

##### Everything follows a cycle

Just as night follows day and day becomes night, our bodies also have natural cycles. For example, in Qigong we nourish and store our energy so that it can be expressed as activity. When we have used up our energy we need to replenish it once more, and in order to be healthy the cycle of storing and giving out energy must be perfectly balanced, so that we don’t become depleted or over-energized.
When we practise Qigong we accumulate and store energy, a Yin process. Energy behaves like a clear, flowing stream. If the energy is blocked, it will stagnate. Free-flowing Qi can be used to repair our bodies, or to expend in the activities of daily life – a Yang process. If we use too much energy we will be depleted and our health will suffer. If we generate and hold on to too much, our health will suffer. Everything in Qigong is designed for a Yin Yang balance of Qi energy.
The moves in Qigong end the way they begin, so that a cycle is travelled and we feel complete.

#### What Makes Qigong Different from Other Exercise?

Qigong is far more than just ordinary exercise. It is made up of many different aspects, and if any part is missing, it’s not Qigong.
These essential qualities interconnect and affect one another. For example, attitude, breathing and relaxation affect your state of mind. Fluidity is not possible without relaxation or without correct posture and breathing. Balance is affected by posture, relaxation and state of mind. A calm state of mind and feeling connected increase confidence and sensitivity, which in turn allows you to be open to change and aware of your own sense of being.
These qualities develop with practice, over time. The hint of a smile when practising works wonders! A smile releases your brain’s feel-good chemicals, encouraging relaxation and other health benefits.
Movements should be as rooted as a tree, as balanced as a cat, as powerful as a surging wave and as free as a soaring eagle.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Total absorption in the present moment.

##### Mindset

Without the correct mindset, it’s not Qigong.
Your attitude in Qigong should be receptive and open. Your mind should be calm, composed and in the present moment. Your concentration should feel light and all-absorbing, like a young child at play.

##### Breathing

Without correct breathing, it’s not Qigong.
Your breathing reveals your state of mind. Soft, rhythmic, abdominal breathing engenders a calm mind. Breathing should be quiet, smooth, even and free-flowing. When your breathing is perfect, health benefits and relaxation are enhanced.

##### Relaxation

Without relaxation, it’s not Qigong.
Relaxation means there is no unnecessary tension held anywhere in your body or mind. Relaxation allows you to be more sensitive and improves awareness of everything around you. Relaxation affects energy flow, circulation and balance.

##### Posture

Without correct posture, it’s not Qigong.
Correct posture puts you in complete harmony with gravity. It means that everything is in the optimum bio-mechanical alignment to allow efficiency of movement with no unnecessary effort. Good posture requires that each vertebra in your spine is perfectly spaced, with no compression at any point.

##### Connection

If you aren’t connected, it’s not Qigong.
Every part of your body should feel connected, like an energetic network. When you place your mental focus at the Lower Dantian, just below your navel, you will eventually feel an integration radiating from this central area to every other part of your body. Connecting to this energy centre cultivates a feeling of security, confidence and power.
NOTE: See Posture and Movement Principles for further clarification of some of these points.

#### Qigong for Health, Martial Prowess and Spiritual Development

Qigong can be subdivided in many ways. A simple way is to look at the three main reasons that people practise Qigong.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Old Chinese illustration showing acupuncture points.

##### Health

Most people practise Qigong for its therapeutic benefits, and also because it is an enjoyable activity that brings general wellbeing. It helps a person become more relaxed and balanced, making the body stronger and more capable of healing itself. All of the Qigong movements in Part 4 of this book are therapeutic.
In Chinese thinking, physical health, emotional health and mental health are all part of the same continuum. In China, Qigong is used in hospitals and clinics alongside Western medicine. The country has conducted many research studies to verify the type of health benefits that Qigong can bring, and in China it is often prescribed as part of an overall health treatment for a multitude of conditions. Traditional Chinese Medicine is accepted worldwide as an alternative medicine choice. Interest has been so significant that in 2014 the US federal government created the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH). Its primary responsibility is to conduct research into alternative health approaches such as Qigong, which are presently being implemented within care settings such as hospitals, hospices and military health facilities across the United States.
According to Traditional Chinese Medicine theory, there are twelve Principal Meridians (energy pathways) plus eight Extraordinary Meridians in the human body, along with numerous minor ones, which form a network of invisible energy conduits throughout the body. These channels have over 400 acupuncture points situated at specific locations along them. If health is to be preserved, a balanced Qi flow must circulate throughout these channels.
There is a growing area of practice called medical Qigong which is popular among alternative medicine healers. Medical Qigong practitioners train in human anatomy and physiology, as well as in Qigong to cultivate their own energy and sensitivity. They prescribe specific exercises for particular conditions, often in combination with acupuncture and other energetic treatments which clear and energize the meridian channels in the body.
If you are interested in medical Qigong, it would be worth referencing the Bibliography and Further Reading section. There are numerous texts that fully explain meridian channels, acupoints and other Traditional Chinese Medicine theories. Many general medical practitioners are becoming increasingly interested in certain aspects of the efficacy of alternative therapies.

##### Martial prowess

Martial artists have always sought ways to improve their fighting skills, both to withstand blows and to condition their bodies against injury. Qigong practice can improve performance in any martial art and in any sport that requires stamina, balance, coordination, speed, flexibility and power.
Some types of martial Qigong are termed “hard” Qigong and can damage health if not accompanied by a calm mind trained in meditation, plus long and patient practice in skilled techniques. Hard Qigong methods are not covered in this book, but many of the Qigong moves that are included have a martial significance. In particular, see Standing like a Post – Zhanzhuang if you wish to increase your martial prowess. Zhanzhuang is considered essential training in martial arts to increase strength, power, resolve and stillness of mind.

##### Spiritual development

Qigong offers a path to greater self-awareness and inner peace. Our everyday thoughts are often circular, in that we recall the same thoughts over and over again and they won’t let us rest. In the East these are referred to as “chattering monkeys” or “wild horses”. Once our breathing and mind are calm, we are able to contemplate and meditate without the “chattering monkeys” obstructing mental clarity.
MERIDIAN CHANNELS
There are twelve Principal Meridians and eight Extraordinary Meridians. You could think of them as rivers of Qi energy that flow throughout the body. When you are healthy, the rivers flow smoothly, distributing life-force energy for optimum health. When the energy is blocked for any reason, the organs and tissues in the affected area suffer. Qigong helps to keep the energy flowing and to reduce and eliminate blockages.
Each of the twelve Principal Meridians is linked with an organ, which it affects. The Yin meridians are: Lung, Heart, Pericardium, Spleen, Kidney, Liver. The Yang meridians are Large Intestine, Small Intestine, Triple Burner, Stomach, Bladder, Gall Bladder.
The eight Extraordinary Meridians are: Conception Vessel, Governing Vessel, Penetrating Vessel, Belt Vessel, Yin Linking Vessel, Yang Linking Vessel, Yin Heel Vessel, Yang Heel Vessel.
There is no one-way-fits-all concept to understand spiritual development, because we all have our own personal concepts, which may not fully agree with conventional thinking. A general viewpoint is that spiritual growth involves a process of inner awakening where we go beyond the limitations of the mind and begin to know who we really are. We begin to understand where truth resides in any situation, without our ego getting in the way. As we develop, our sense of inner strength increases, as does our ability to deal honestly and responsibly with everyday life without fear and anxiety. Life becomes more harmonious.
If this is a subject that appeals to you, have a look at the Qigong Meditation chapter. All Qigong exercises interconnect with spiritual development, if practised with a calm mind and attention in the present moment.

##### Health, martial and spiritual categories interconnect

If you practise Qigong mainly for health, you will be enhancing your energy and stamina, which are qualities you need for martial ability. If you practise it in order to increase your martial ability or for spiritual development, your health will improve. And if you practise for martial ability or health in a mindful way, you will gradually become mentally calm and increase your ability to focus your mind. A calm mind is essential for spiritual development. There are no clear-cut defining lines between these categories, as they all overlap.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Old Chinese illustration of men in martial combat.

#### Qigong Meditation

I have been practising meditation since I was 16 years old, but am I any good at it? Well, that’s a little like asking whether you are any good at sleeping. If the surrounding conditions are right and the intention is there, it just happens, like falling asleep just happens. Meditation makes me feel more in tune with the symphony of life. It allows me to put things into perspective and to be more conscious of what is truly important.
The author seated in meditation.

##### What is meditation?

Meditation is quietening the mind while in a tranquil, open state of being. There are different levels of meditation: some are lighter levels where you are aware of everything around you, and some are deeper levels where your sense of time and ego disappear. All levels increase awareness of your inner nature and engender an appreciation of being in the present moment.
China’s tradition of meditation is as rich as India’s, and is mentioned in many ancient Chinese writings.
The word meditation is rooted in Sanskrit, Greek and Latin. The Latin verb meditari means to contemplate, think over, reflect. The Latin verb mederi means to heal, and it is comforting and enlightening to know that the idea of healing lies within the roots of the word “meditation”.
All Qigong practice has a meditative quality. At first you may not be aware that you are engaging in the initial stages of meditation, but whenever you focus all of your attention on what you are doing, you will begin to notice that your breathing becomes soft and rhythmic and your mind calm.
From a scientific point of view, meditation is a state where brain waves slow down. Brain waves are divided into four types: Beta, Alpha, Theta and Delta. Each type has a different wave pattern and can be measured on an electroencephalogram (EEG), which is a recording of brain activity.
Beta, with 15–40 waves per second, is our everyday state when awake and active. This state is associated with fast, logical thinking and high levels of alertness.
Alpha, with 8–15 waves per second, is our relaxed, peaceful, creative state of mind. It is associated with light meditation, concentration and enhanced learning capability.
Theta, with 4–8 waves per second, is a state that occurs in deeper relaxation and meditation, and also in light sleep and dreaming. It is a very receptive, intuitive state where inspiration and insight occur.
Delta, with 0.5–4 waves per second, is the state of deep, dreamless sleep and deep meditation. Delta is associated with the unconscious mind, and usually only experienced meditators reach this state. Some say it is the gateway to the universal mind.
Our bodies heal and regenerate when the brain is in the Theta and Delta signal frequencies, and this is one reason that high-quality sleep is essential to our health. Meditation acts in a similar way to quality sleep, but while we are awake.

##### Why meditate?

It is possible for us to take responsibility for our own state of mind: to calm it, improve it and create a more positive reality. Meditation produces a state of deep inner relaxation, while at the same time stabilizing the mind and creating stronger Qi, or life force. In addition, meditation encourages personal and spiritual growth. It has a positive and balancing effect on a person’s mental state and relieves conditions such as stress, anxiety, sleep disorders and depression, all of which contribute to a multitude of medical conditions. Meditation can also improve memory, confidence, insight, mental focus, mental clarity and possibly longevity.
If your mind is full of emotional turmoil, never-ending worries, problems and agitation, you will have little inclination, time or ability to extend energy and compassion toward others. Being constantly in a state of anxiety, stress and tension uses up a large proportion of a person’s energy, and that means there isn’t much energy left over to offer to others, to help with their needs and problems.
Benefits are cumulative, and even as little as 10 to 20 minutes’ meditation a day, on a regular basis, can have a profound effect in your daily life. The Daoists have a saying that a true man walks in meditation, which means that it is possible for us to proceed throughout daily life with composure and a peaceful state of mind.
Meditation brings with it a sense of freedom as well as a sense of belonging to something greater than ourselves.

##### First steps to meditation

1 Breathing: Concentrate on soft abdominal breathing, like the perfect breathing of a young child. The way you breathe affects your body and mind.
2 Relaxation: Do a few relaxation, warm-up or stretching exercises (see Warm-ups). Qigong exercises are an ideal preparation, as they gently lubricate and loosen all the joints and tissues of the body and calm the mind.
3 Posture: Whether you decide to stand or to sit on the floor or a chair, your spine should be extended, with no compression along any part of the spinal column. Imagine that your spine is lengthening so that the spaces between the vertebrae increase and you feel you are growing taller. From the waist up, feel that your body is so light and balanced, it almost seems as though it is floating. Your chin should be level to the ground, jaw relaxed, back of the throat feeling open. Your sitting should feel grounded through the seat bones and your standing should feel grounded through the feet. (See Posture and Movement Principles)
4 Tip of tongue: With your lips lightly touching each other, place the tip of your tongue lightly on the upper palate (roof of your mouth), just behind your upper teeth. This encourages saliva flow, which lubricates the throat. If your throat is dry, your body won’t be able to relax completely. The position also makes it easy for the jaw to relax – if your jaw is clenched, it tenses your face, neck and shoulder muscles. This tip-of-tongue position joins the Conception Vessel Meridian, which is Yin, and the Governing Vessel Meridian, which is Yang, thereby joining Yin and Yang together energetically.
5 Eyes: Your eyes can be closed or open. Closed eyes filter out distractions more effectively, but if closing your eyes makes you feel dizzy or disoriented, keep them open. If open, look slightly downward, so that you are looking at the floor ahead of you. Sometimes when we look down there is a tendency to drop the head a little, so beware of this – drop the eyelids, not the head.
Eyes can be closed or open with eyelids lowered.
6 Attention: Focus your attention on your chosen object (see Methods) for an extended length of time. If you are new to this, a minute might seem like a long time, but if you practise regularly, you will have no problem in eventually retaining your concentration for up to ten, even 20 minutes or longer. If you give all of your attention to one specific thing, all extraneous thoughts tend to slip into the background or temporarily disappear altogether.
WHAT IF MY MIND WON’T REST?
When you first begin, it is normal for the constant replay of your thoughts to continue their chattering within your head. Treat your mind like you would a very young child whose attention is wandering, and keep bringing him or her back to the task at hand. Eventually you will have built up a good habit, and with patience, love and direction, your much loved “child” will gain the ability to concentrate.

##### Methods

There are a great many meditation methods to choose from and they all have the same purpose: to create mental focus. Different schools promote their own favourites. No method is necessarily better than another, but some might suit you better than others. A selection is given here. Initially, following a method is important, so that you have a structure within which to focus your mind. Eventually, dependence on the method becomes less of a need, and fades into the background when deeper levels of meditation are reached.
You need only one method, but it is good to have an overview so that you have an appreciation of different approaches. The examples given here are for light forms of meditation, which consist of attention and concentration exercises to train your mind, but which also have a deep relaxation response.
Attention on the breath: There are multiple variations of meditation focusing on the breath, but one of the easiest and most popular techniques is to place your attention on your inhalation and exhalation and be aware of the movement that occurs in your body with the action of each breath.
Counting: This could be as simple as slowly counting from ten to one, or even from one hundred down to zero. A counting exercise that I use is to count from eleven to zero, and every time a thought appears between a count, return to eleven again. If you manage to reach zero, allow the mind to remain floating at the space around zero until a new thought arises, at which time you start again at eleven.
Sound: There are many ways to use sound. Some people use gongs, brass bowls, crystal bowls or various types of music to create a pleasing sound and vibration. Listening to the sounds of nature – for example, birdsong, trees in the wind, waves on the shore – can be forms of meditation if you give all of your attention to the sound.
Chanting: Repeating a mantra or chant over and over again is a time-honoured tradition in many cultures, including Qigong. The chant can be repeated out loud or silently to yourself. Chanting can be done either alone or in a group. The gentle, continuous vibration and repetition of the chant bring peace to the mind.
Prayer beads: Beads threaded together on a string are used in a number of different religions as a focal point for devotion. The number of beads is often symbolic, with different traditions using numbers symbolic to them, for example 18, 27, 54, 108. People who are not religious also use beads as a concentration tool. A set chant is repeated at each bead. This method offers the security of ritual and a steady framework within which to meditate.
Visualization: The variations of visualization are as endless as the imagination of the meditator or the tradition being drawn from. Visualization is often combined with breathing, for example creating a visualized route for the breath (see Microcosmic Orbit).
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
Each stone has its own character, texture, colour and balance.
Attention on an energy centre: In Qigong we place our attention on energy centres called Dantians. The energy is called Qi. There are three main Dantians: Lower, Middle and Upper. In Yoga, we place our attention on energy centres called Chakras. The energy is called Prana, but it is the same as Qi. There are seven main Chakras: Root, Sacral, Navel/Solar Plexus, Heart, Throat, Brow and Crown.
Attention on an object or colour: Any pleasing object can be used, but objects from nature such as a pebble from a beach or a leaf are usually easier to relate to. Different colours have different vibrations, and if no particular colour is specified, use a colour that resonates with you.
Single-pointed attention: Place your attention at the Lower Dantian for longer and longer lengths of time, according to your concentration capacity. Meditation can be completely at this area during a dedicated time span. However, it is a common practice for martial artists to place half of their attention at the Lower Dantian while going about their daily life. This practice has a de-focusing effect on random thoughts and disruptive emotions and creates stability and calm. When the mind is quiet, you become more aware of everything around you.
Mandala: This is a drawing or design that usually reflects or symbolizes the cosmos and is used as a focus for contemplation. In some cultures, sand is a favourite medium because it reflects the impermanence of existence in that it can be brushed away so easily. In other cultures a permanent and well-known mandala is used. You could use the Yin Yang symbol as a mandala.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
A mandala full of symbolism.
Walking: People walk in a labyrinth, in a circle, in the forest or mountains or in any quiet place where there is the security of a known route. A labyrinth is a circular path that winds its way into a centre. The walker uses the same path to return, and so the entrance becomes the exit. Any circular path can be seen as a metaphor for the path we walk in life, and many people find it has a restorative and calming effect. The Qigong exercise Walking on Clouds is performed in a circle and can be used as a walking meditation practice.
Candle gazing: The tradition of gazing at a flame probably began when man first lit a candle or fire. The image of the flame can be taken into the mind’s eye to be held as an inner flame at the Upper Dantian spot between the eyebrows. Some people visualize a flame without need of a candle.
Stargazing: We have all looked up and gazed at the stars, but these days only a few of us spend any length of time stargazing as our ancestors once did before the advent of electricity, television and computers. The vastness of space brings us a sense of childlike awe and wonder, and to lose ourselves for a while in this deep space imbues us with a sense of eternity. To the ancient Chinese, stars had great symbolic attachments and much time was spent in stargazing.
Metaphor: This is a form of visualization where an image, usually taken from nature, is used as a symbol. A classic example is visualizing a lake and likening it to your mind. The visualization of a clear, deep, smooth lake is calming. When the surface of the lake is clear like a mirror, observing it reflects our true spiritual nature back to us.
Contemplation: A certain quality, ideal or philosophical statement is observed with an open, attentive mind. For example, what is loving kindness, what is its vibration, how is it best expressed? This type of meditation often leads to deeper understanding of life’s most important questions.
Watching your thoughts: Watch your thoughts pass by at a distance, with no judgement or comment. When your thoughts appear at longer and longer intervals, move your attention to the spaces between the thoughts. The spaces are deeply calming and sometimes expand for long periods of time.
Create space: At the Middle or Upper Dantian, feel the energy expand, creating a sense of spaciousness. When things are going wrong in our lives, we can sometimes feel that we are contracting inward and closing down. The expansive, spacious feeling created with this meditation is very uplifting and helps us to expand outward, so that we no longer feel hemmed in by life events or narrow thinking patterns.
Moving meditation: Qigong meditation can be done while moving. Practise any easy Qigong move and perform it in a slow, flowing manner with complete attention so that no other thoughts enter your mind, and you will create a tranquil, meditative state which becomes “moving meditation”. Other traditions use dance, either with form or freestyle, to instil a sense of complete absorption of the dancer into the dance.
Mindfulness: This is the daily practice of paying attention to what we are doing, while we are doing it, without any distraction from extraneous thoughts. Thoughts from the past or future disconnect us, preventing us from being in the present, and that means we could end up living a large part of our lives in our heads, rather than right now in the world, in the present moment.
Transparency: At the Middle or Upper Dantian, create a sense of spaciousness. Extend this feeling of space to every part of your body, or even to every cell if your imagination can extend to this. Feel that you are so spacious inside that you are almost transparent, and that every sound, emotion and thought can now pass through you without obstruction. Once you become accustomed to this practice, things such as unwanted sounds or negative energy in daily life will no longer trouble you.

##### Spiritual development

We all have our own personal interpretations of what spiritual development means. The following is merely my interpretation and, as for most people, it will probably change over time.
We all go through stages of development, and some of us want to stay at a certain stage, for our own reasons, and this should be respected. No stage should be rushed. In our youth, most of us are self-centred and might display manipulative, selfish behaviour and a lack of awareness of anything outside of our own needs and experience. If we grow beyond this stage we start to develop selflessness and compassion, and are able to discipline our personal desires so they do not harm or deprive others.
Further progression involves looking into our own minds and hearts for answers to the important questions of life, rather than accepting someone else’s interpretation. This stage requires a lot of confidence about our own personal identity, as the certainties of life can seem to disappear. This is why many people find it easier to stay in a cosy, secure, but limited mental place with fixed ideas. Sometimes we may feel alone and deserted because no one understands our personal search for a wider worldview. Our childhood belief systems may start to seem inadequate as we mature and begin to look beyond our own background, culture or country. We might become cynical or feel superior, rejecting the things of our past, especially if conflict is involved.
If we are able to progress through this stage, we can look within ourselves for a deeper connection to all life, and start to view ourselves as connected to something greater, perhaps divine or beyond our current understanding. When we establish a true connection, we no longer feel alone or afraid, and begin to understand why people are the way they are, without the all too common inclination to judge, condemn or feel superior. We understand the need to realize that we all inhabit the world equally, together, and our sense of brotherhood with all life expands.
This stage leads us to want further development, fuelled by a curiosity to explore the limits of the human mind beyond what reason and logic can offer. We understand the cosmic joke of attempting to explore our current limits with a mind that is intrinsically limited, and enjoy nudging the boundaries, comfortable with the knowledge that there is no certainty, except perhaps change itself.
Once we open our minds to see the unity in all things, even divergent ideas, and start to understand the feeling and sensing of things, we realize the need to let go of our deeply embedded conceit and superficial identity. Once the ego lets go of its limpet hold, we realize that the ego is a separator, and things that once seemed essential no longer have value. Love and gratitude grow, forgiveness is natural and dealing with uncertainty is not such an issue.
As the feeling of connection with all things increases, so does trust in our own intuition and acceptance of the universal plan – whatever that may be. This freedom from ego bestows deep confidence and at the same time melts away self-importance. A feeling of spiritual oneness with something greater than ourselves continues to grow, bringing with it a true sense of inner peace that is serene, energizing and fascinating. And so the journey continues to the next level, wherever and whatever that may be.

##### Qigong meditation exercises

The following three well-known Qigong meditation practices instil a sense of calm and peace and have a cleansing quality. All three are performed in a state of light meditation, and awareness of what is around you is maintained.

##### The Microcosmic Orbit

The Microcosmic Orbit refers to a Qigong method for circulating energy around a circuit of two meridian channels. The Conception Vessel (Ren Mai) channel runs down the front of the body. The Governing Vessel (Du Mai) channel runs up the back of the body. The joining points for the two channels are at the perineum (the area between the anus and the genitals) and at the roof of the mouth.
The practice has a long history, and references appear in the Yijing c. 1000 BCE. The Daoists considered it to be a first step toward cultivating the golden elixir of immortality. They believed that if you circulated the energy along the Microcosmic Orbit as a daily practice, chronic physical ailments would disappear. They would practise even while walking and had a saying that a true man walks in meditation.
1 Take a sitting or standing position that is comfortable. See the three positions that follow for Clear Brow of the Sage, and choose your favourite. Close your eyes or lower your eyelids. Feel that your upper body is light, with the spine extended. Place the tip of your tongue on your upper palate, behind the teeth. Breathe with deep, soft abdominal breaths, through your nose, until your breathing has become naturally quiet, slow, fine and light, with a continuous, subtle, soothing rhythm. Continue to place attention on your breathing until your mind is calm.
2 Focus your attention at the Lower Dantian for a few minutes and feel that the Qi energy is merged with your breath. When you feel ready to begin, inhale softly and visualize the breath travelling from the meeting place of your tongue and upper palate, down the front of your body to the perineum. As you exhale, imagine Qi travelling up the back of your body along your spine, over the crown of your head and down to where your tongue touches the palate. This is one breath cycle. The inhalation is Yin energy, the energy of earth. The exhalation is Yang energy, the energy of heaven. Begin with 10 breath cycles and gradually work up to 30 minutes or more.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
The Microcosmic Orbit
Variations: There are different ways of circulating the Qi in the Microcosmic Orbit, but until you have a basic route established, as described earlier, variations can be counterproductive. One variation is to reverse the breathing direction. Another is to visualize significant acupoints along the Microcosmic Orbit. However, to practise variations prematurely can lead to energy blocks and disturbances – the exact opposite of the primary purpose of the exercise, which is to promote Qi energy flow. Once the Microcosmic Orbit has become natural to you, another variation is the Macrocosmic Orbit, which includes the arms and legs. Variations should not be attempted without the guidance of an experienced teacher.

##### Clear Brow of the Sage

The name of this meditation implies that a person of wisdom does not have a furrowed brow or worry lines across the forehead because he or she has learned the art of calm and the attitude of open acceptance. Give this a try and become a sage for a moment in time. This is one of my favourite meditations, which I often teach at the end of classes while everyone stands in Holding a Tree position for about five minutes. Every one of us can achieve this clear brow for a few minutes, and I have seen some students extending the skill for longer periods of time, some even throughout a significant part of their day.
1 This exercise can be done sitting or standing. If standing, take a Shoulder-width Stance and have your hands folded over the Lower Dantian. If you are feeling stronger, stand in a Horse Stance in the Holding a Tree position. If seated, sit with a straight back with feet apart and the soles of your feet in contact with the floor; resting your hands on your thighs allows your arms to relax.
Addition of an inner smile: Sometimes we add an inner smile. Imagine a gently curved smile positioned between your eyebrows and inside your head. On each exhalation imagine the corners of the smile pushing the eyebrows slightly further apart. Don’t be surprised if a hint of a smile touches your mouth and you start to feel happy and at peace.
2 Begin by placing your attention on your abdominal breathing, until it feels slow, calm and rhythmic. Now lead your inner vision to the Upper Dantian between your eyebrows. Expand the area between your eyebrows by releasing tense muscles, and extend this feeling to include the whole of the forehead, brow and temples. Look into the Upper Dantian with your inner vision and, as more and more tension releases, you will experience a feeling of expansion. To an observer you will appear peaceful and your brow area will appear clear of worry lines. Hold your focus at the Upper Dantian as though you are looking into a place of infinite space. This posture can be held for any length of time from one minute to half an hour or more.
TRAINING THE BROW MUSCLES
Some people are unable to expand the forehead because there is a muscle memory of tension that does not initially respond to easing and smoothing requests from the brain. If this is the case with your forehead, place your fingers between your eyebrows and gently pull the flesh outward, tracing your brow line with your fingertips until they rest at your temples. Hold your fingertips at your temples for a few seconds.
Repeat the exercise several times. On your last repetition, lift your fingertips away from your temples and try to hold the open feeling of relaxed brow and forehead muscles. You may have to train your brow muscles repeatedly – they behave in the same manner as any other group of muscles that are used to being held repeatedly with tension, and will respond to gentle, consistent reminding.

##### Qi Washing

The idea of this meditation is that you can wash away physical and mental tensions and blockages, head to toe, using visualization or feeling, led by your intention. Recently, I met a student from many years ago and I asked him if he still practised Qigong. He said that the only thing he still practised almost every day was Qi Washing because it eased his emotional problems and made him feel mentally clean.
Qi Washing
Qi Washing is best done standing, so that the feeling of gravity aids the washing process. Stand in a Shoulder-width Stance with arms held loosely at your sides and your eyes closed.
Place your attention on slow, rhythmic, abdominal breathing until you feel calm and centred. Choose an appropriate image for the washing process: it could be an image of water or golden light or a colour that feels right. Whichever image you choose, feel that it is imbued with Qi energy. Move your attention to above the top of your head and feel the water, light or colour start to fall very, very slowly through your body, washing away any tension or blockage in your muscles, emotions or mind. Gradually the washing makes its way downward through your feet and into the ground beneath.
Visualizing the washing process is good, but feeling it is even better. Allow the cleansing to reach every small area of your being. Spend a minimum of two minutes and repeat several times if you wish. It is common to feel refreshed and relaxed at the end.

#### Basic Stances

Your stance is the way you stand – how you place your feet and how you distribute your weight – and is the foundation for every Qigong move. It must be steady, balanced and rooted to the ground so that the upper body can be light and agile, just as the base of a tree must be rooted to the earth so that the upper trunk and branches are free to move with the wind. The seven fundamental stances required in order to perform all of the Qigong exercises in this book are shown in this chapter.

##### No. 1 Shoulder-width Stance

This is sometimes called a Parallel Stance, because the feet are parallel to each other. It is your most important stance because most movements begin and end with this stance. It can be used as a resting stance, as well as an opening and closing stance.
Place your feet so they are the width of your own shoulders apart, with your feet parallel and your knees relaxed.
Some people have much wider shoulders than others, and so their stance might look wider than yours. Always pay attention to your own body build, or you could end up with a stance suitable for your teacher, but not for you! An anatomically strong position is where the feet are directly in line with the hip joints so that there is a vertical line of force from the hip joints down through the knee and ankle joints. However, some people prefer a wider stance because a wider base provides more stability. Also, women often have larger hips than men, and many teachers advise using hip width or shoulder width, whichever is wider.
It is common for people to put more weight on their stronger leg, without being aware of it, so do your best to distribute your weight evenly – 50 per cent of your weight on each foot. Your knees should be in good alignment with your toes, which means they should be pointing in the same direction as your toes. When bending your knees, they must not project beyond your toes because this is a weak position that could damage your knee joints. You should be able to feel each toe in contact with the ground, and the inner and outer heel edges should also be in contact with the ground.
The Bubbling Spring point, Yongquan (see The Bubbling Spring), should be in contact with the ground to provide an energetic feeling of connection and rooting.
THE BUBBLING SPRING
The Yongquan or Bubbling Spring is the first acupoint on the Kidney Meridian channel. “Yong” means gush, well up, surge, and “quan” means a spring or fountain. The feet should not pronate (roll inward) or supinate (roll outward). The Bubbling Spring point should be in contact with the ground in all standing positions, and also when walking.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

##### Starting posture

Shoulder-width Stance, with arms held loosely by your sides, is used as your starting posture for most Qigong moves. By beginning this way, you give yourself a chance to bring your attention to your posture and connection to the ground, and also to compose your mind.
Starting posture.

###### Postural reminders

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and parallel to each other.
Feel that your ankle, knee and hip joints are aligned.
Your knees should feel soft, not locked. “Soft” means that there is a hint of a bend in the knees.
Feel as though your spine is fluid like a string of pearls.
Feel as though your upper body is light and floating from the waist up.
Feel as though your lower body is heavy and rooted from the waist down.
Relax your whole body, especially your shoulders, arms and hands.
Imagine a weight on your tailbone, grounding you to the earth.
Imagine your head suspended from above by a golden thread attached from the crown of your head up to a cloud in the sky, so that the back of your neck feels gently stretched upward without feeling fixed.
Look forward with soft, relaxed eyes.
Keep your chin level to the ground.
Touch the tip of your tongue to the roof of your mouth and relax your jaw.
Expand your forehead and brow, and relax your mind.
Feel natural and in harmony with gravity.

##### Closing posture

Shoulder-width Stance is used in the closing posture for each Qigong move or set of moves. By ending this way, you give yourself a feeling of completion and a feeling of having cultivated and stored energy.
Gather up Qi energy with a circular motion of your hands and bring it to the Lower Dantian, which is an energy field approximately 5cm (2in) below your navel, inside your body at your centre of gravity. Over time you will cultivate a store of vital energy.
Women place the right hand on first, with the left hand on top, just below the navel. Men place the left hand on first, with the right hand on top, just below the navel.
Closing posture.

##### No. 2 Horse Stance

This is sometimes called Horse-riding Stance because it looks like the position you would take when riding a horse. This stance is known for strengthening all of the muscles in both legs equally and especially for strengthening the muscles around the knees. It is highly valued in all martial arts for training and conditioning purposes.
GOLDEN RULE FOR KNEES
Whichever stance you are practising, remember the golden rule for good knee safety and alignment: the knees should be in the same direction as your toes and should never project beyond your toes.
Bend both knees and step out to the side with your left foot to a position slightly wider than shoulder width. Your toes can be turned out by about 10 degrees. This slight turning out takes pressure off the knees and is recommended by osteopaths. Some people feel more comfortable with a larger turn-out, but no more than 30 degrees maximum or you lose the strength of the stance. Bend your knees out to the sides, not forward. Feel as though you are sitting on a horse. Keep your back vertical and feel your weight go down through your heels.
Horse Stances are performed at different widths: small, medium or large. A small Horse Stance is a tiny bit wider than a Shoulder-width Stance. A medium Horse Stance is noticeably wider than shoulder-width. A large Horse Stance has the feet as wide apart as half of your height, or even wider, and requires a considerable amount of muscle flexibility and strength to hold for any length of time.
Horse Stances are performed at different heights: high, medium-height or low. The lower you hold the stance, the more challenging it becomes. A high Horse Stance has the knees bent by only a small amount. The low, large Horse Stance is performed with thighs almost parallel to the ground. This requires strength, hip and muscle flexibility and a good understanding of alignment so as not to damage the lower back or knees.
If you have never practised a Horse Stance before, it is best to start in a small, high stance.

##### No. 3 Back Stance

This stance takes its name from the fact that most of your weight is on the back leg. Sometimes it is called an Empty Stance, because the front leg is empty of weight. A Back Stance is usually considered a defensive position.
Start in a Shoulder-width Stance, bend both knees, transfer 70–90 per cent of your weight onto your right leg, and then place your left leg forward. The back leg knee should remain bent and the front knee should be slightly bent. Keep your back erect. Repeat on the other side.
The stance can be performed with the front ankle flexed up, so that the toes on the front foot are lifted.
Alternatively, the front foot can be flat on the ground, dependent upon the move and the style.
If you are new to this stance, place only 70 per cent of your weight on the back leg and bend your back knee only as far as is comfortable.

##### No. 4 Cat Stance

This stance gets its name from the nature of the cat. When a cat is stalking, it often puts a front paw lightly forward to test the ground and ensure that all conditions are right, before either transferring its weight or leaping forward at its prey.
From a Shoulder-width Stance, transfer all of your weight to your right leg and bend your right knee. Place the toes of your left foot lightly on the floor. The front knee should be slightly bent and feel as though it is being lifted upward – this is called a “nimble” knee because it allows you to change quickly into either another stance or a kick. Keep almost all of your weight on the back leg. Repeat on the other side.
Cat Stances can be high or low. Low stances have the knees bent more and the front foot is placed further away.
If you have never done this stance before, keep your front step small so that the toes are close to your other foot, and keep your stance high.

##### No. 5 Nail Stance

The name of this stance comes from its resemblance to a nail being hammered into the floor. The nail is strong and straight, and when the toes of one foot are in this position, they add strength and balance to your stance. It is used as a transitional stance to keep your balance before proceeding to the next move.
Transfer almost all of your weight to the right leg. Bring your left toes to rest beside your right foot, but without your feet touching each other, and bend both knees. Lift your left heel as high as possible so that your foot becomes vertical, like a nail going into the ground. Repeat on the other side.
The Nail Stance can be performed with the balls of the toes on the ground, or with just the tips of the toes lightly touching the ground. It can be performed in a high stance or a low stance.
If this stance is new to you, start with the balls of the toes on the ground in a high stance. Whenever you are on one leg, you can use this stance to help keep your balance.

##### No. 6 Crane Stance

The crane is a symbol of longevity in China. It is also associated with swiftness, grace and elegance. The crane has great endurance to stand on one leg effortlessly over long periods of time. The Crane Stance is meant to look elegant and balanced.
Start in a Shoulder-width Stance. Transfer your weight to your right leg, and lift your left knee as high as possible, in front of you. Point the toes downward and allow the foot to naturally turn inward toward your centreline. In training for martial arts, the front leg is ready both to kick and to defend against kicks. In training for health, the stance teaches strength, elegance and balance. Repeat on the other side.
If this stance is new to you, lift the knee only as high as is comfortable, even if this means that your toes are close to the ground. As your balance and strength improve, try lifting the knee higher.

##### No. 7 Bow Stance

The front leg is an allusion to the curved front part of the bow and the back leg is straight like the drawstring of the bow. Occasionally it takes the name Mountain Climbing Stance because it resembles the action of lunging forward when climbing a steep hill or mountain. Some schools call it Front Stance or Forward Stance, because most of the weight is on the front leg.
Place your left foot one step ahead, bend your front knee and transfer 70–90 per cent of your weight forward.
Keep your knees in line with your toes. The soles of both feet should be firmly planted on the ground. Repeat on the other side.
Some schools have the back foot turned out at a 45-degree angle. Other schools have the back foot parallel to the front foot.
If you have never done this stance before, bring no more than 70 per cent of your weight forward.

##### Moving between stances

Moving from stance to stance is a good way to train your strength, balance and agility. Qigong exercises often move back and forth between Back Stance and Bow Stance. A traditional martial arts strengthening exercise is to move between Nail Stance and Horse Stance, side to side, for many repetitions. Vary the order of the stances when you practise. A good test of whether you know the stances is to have a friend call out the stance names in an unpredictable order, and see how smoothly you can move from one stance to another. Your stance is your foundation, and the more familiar you are with the basic stances, the more easily you will be able to learn any Qigong move.

#### Breathing

##### The breath of life

Breathing is essential to life. Correct breathing increases energy, reduces anxiety and rejuvenates your body. The most important breathing technique is abdominal breathing, which should be your everyday breathing method.

##### Breath of a child

This is also called abdominal breathing, belly breathing, natural breathing and Buddhist breathing.
As we get older, many of us restrict our breathing to the upper chest using short, shallow breaths. This is not nourishing to our bodies or minds.
When a young, healthy child breathes, the whole torso expands on each inhalation. It is effortless and perfect, and the child’s energy seems inexhaustible. But as we age, the stresses and tensions of daily life take their toll. The diaphragm becomes sluggish, the intercostal muscles (the muscles between the ribs) become stiff and breathing efficiency starts to diminish.
Watch the breathing of a healthy child who is young enough that the stresses of life have not yet taken their toll. Babies and young children breathe in and out through their noses. They breathe softly, smoothly and continuously, expanding and contracting the whole of the abdomen. The chest, belly, ribcage and back are mobile, expanding with each inhalation and contracting with each exhalation. When you watch them breathe, you feel you are watching the rhythm of life. Let them be your guides.
The sweet smell of Qi.
Many adults don’t even realize that their breathing is shallow and restricted to the upper chest. During my time working in a mental-health unit teaching Qigong and yoga, I always included improving the way clients breathed. It was one of the most transforming parts of their practice. They were often amazed to find they could lower their blood pressure, manage asthma, prevent anxiety attacks and feel more peaceful simply by improving their breathing. Abdominal breathing also improves the resonance of your voice and allows you to express yourself more fully in speaking or singing. Breathing abdominally massages the internal organs, improving digestion and circulation.
THE VAGUS NERVE
This is the body’s longest nerve, running through the brain, chest, diaphragm, intestines and organs. It is the main part of our parasympathetic nervous system and communicates with our brain through neurotransmitters. Abdominal breathing soothes the vagus nerve, which then sends messages to the brain to stimulate the relaxation response. This helps to relax and slow down our breathing rate, as well as improving our immune and nervous systems. It helps us to overcome depression and anxiety, and stimulates cell regeneration.
With advances in neuroscience, we now know that a large part of our feel-good hormones such as dopamine and serotonin are produced in the gut and that gut dysfunction is responsible for a much wider range of maladies than previously realized. Breathing abdominally helps to keep your “gut brain” happy.

##### How to breath abdominally

What if you are someone who has never thought about breathing abdominally? No problem! It’s easy to learn.
The main muscle used in inhalation, the diaphragm, is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle under your lungs. When you breathe in using your full lung capacity, this muscle contracts and the dome flattens out and pushes downward, expanding your abdomen.
It’s much easier to start lying down, but eventually you will feel confident enough to try abdominal breathing while sitting and standing. Your breath rate will naturally start to slow down and you will become more peaceful.

##### Breathe to a count to regulate the breath

When you have become accustomed to abdominal breathing, try breathing to a count. Breathe in to a count of four, pause for a second and then breathe out to a count of four.

##### Abdominal Breathing

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
1 Lie down on the floor with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. This position will prevent your lower back from over-arching. Put a pillow under your head if this makes you feel more comfortable, and place your hands on your belly with fingertips touching. If you are unable to lie on the floor, lie on a bed. Breathe in deeply through your nose and then sigh aloud saying, “Ahhhh!” as you exhale.
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
2 Wait patiently for your body to breathe in, rather than initiating the inhalation yourself. Your first inhalation after the sigh will be a true abdominal breath and you will feel it expanding your abdomen; your hands will separate with the expansion. Your ribcage will also expand, and if you are lying on the floor, you might feel your back expanding. You may not feel a lot of expansion at first because unused breathing muscles may have gone to sleep for a decade or two, but if you practise they will wake up.
Some teachers may advise breathing in through the nose and out through the mouth. The reason is that breathing out through a small space between your lips can make you more conscious of your breathing pattern, but as you progress you will no longer need to breathe out through your mouth.
Breathing to a count helps to shift your focus away from worries, concerns and even pain, and brings your focus to the smooth rhythm of your breathing. When your mind is still and your breathing is natural, you will no longer need to think about your breathing. However, it can take up to six months, and sometimes longer, to become instinctively proficient in abdominal breathing.

##### Other types of breathing

In addition to abdominal breathing, there are other methods of breathing, a few of which are briefly covered here. However, they are beyond the requirements of most people, but abdominal breathing is a prerequisite.

##### Dantian breathing

This is similar to abdominal breathing, but lower and more subtle. This breathing stimulates the kidneys and lower spine and increases the body’s overall energy level. It increases the relaxation response, which helps you to react better to stress.
Locate the lowest place where your abdomen expansion originates. This is different for everyone because it is dependent upon body proportions. For some it will be as high as the navel, and for others as low as just above the pubic bone. Place your attention at the lowest point of expansion, including your lower back so that you become aware of expansion around your lower back and kidneys on the inhalation, and contraction on the exhalation.

##### Reverse breathing

This is sometimes referred to as Daoist breathing. Mastery of abdominal breathing is a prerequisite. Often used by martial arts experts, reverse breathing stimulates the Qi energy and allows the practitioner to lead Qi more efficiently to any part of the body.
When you inhale, pull the abdomen gently inward; when you exhale, push the abdomen gently outward. This is the reverse of abdominal breathing and should not be done for long periods of time. If done incorrectly, it can cause medical problems, including tension in the abdomen, pressure in the chest area and a rise in blood pressure. If you decide to train in this type of breathing, find a competent instructor.

##### Embryonic breathing

This is also known as internal, primordial or umbilical breathing. It refers to a state of breathing that is so subtle that to an observer it might appear as though the person has stopped breathing. In meditation, embryonic breathing often happens spontaneously as the meditator’s mind becomes free of thoughts and enters a state of complete serenity.
Bring yourself to a state of calm with slow abdominal breathing. Feel that the breath is entering and leaving through your whole body with no effort from you.
